mass-energy.name: Mass-energy equivalence
mass-energy.oneLiner: The formula showing that mass and energy convert into each other at the rate of the speed of light squared
mass-energy.description: An equation that comes out of Einstein's special relativity. It shows that mass can turn into energy and energy into mass, and that the exchange rate is the speed of light squared. Because that square is so large, even a small mass can release an enormous amount of energy.
mass-energy.significance: By revealing that mass is itself a form of energy, it changed the paradigm of modern physics, and it explains how nuclear fission and fusion work.

E.description: The energy the object holds. Units: joules (J).

m.description: The rest mass of the object. Units: kilograms (kg).

c.description: The speed of light in a vacuum. About 3×10⁸ m/s.

c^2.role: Square of the speed of light
c^2.description: About 9×10¹⁶. It is the mass-energy conversion rate.

newton-second.name: Newton's second law of motion
newton-second.oneLiner: The law that the force acting on a body equals its mass times its acceleration
newton-second.description: Newton's second law states that the net force on a body is its mass times its acceleration. For the same force, the greater the mass the smaller the acceleration, which is how mass quantifies inertia. It is the most central equation of motion in classical mechanics.
newton-second.significance: By establishing the quantitative relation between force, mass, and acceleration, it laid the foundation of classical mechanics.

F.description: The net force acting on the body. Units: newtons (N).

m.description: The mass of the body. It measures its inertia. Units: kg.

a.description: The rate at which velocity changes with time. Units: m/s².

universal-gravitation.name: Law of universal gravitation
universal-gravitation.oneLiner: The law that two bodies attract each other with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of their separation
universal-gravitation.description: The law of universal gravitation says that every body with mass attracts every other, with a force proportional to the product of the two masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them. It was a revolutionary law, uniting the fall of an apple and the orbit of the Moon under a single principle.
universal-gravitation.significance: By uniting celestial motion with terrestrial mechanics, it established the first universal law of physics.

F.description: The attractive force between the two bodies. Units: newtons (N).

G.description: The constant of universal gravitation. About 6.674×10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg².

m_1.description: The mass of the first of the interacting bodies.

m_2.description: The mass of the second of the interacting bodies.

r.description: The distance between the centres of mass of the two bodies.

r^2.description: It carries the inverse-square law. Double the distance and the force falls to a quarter.

coulomb-law.name: Coulomb's law
coulomb-law.oneLiner: The law that the electric force between two charges is proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of their separation
coulomb-law.description: Coulomb's law states that the electric force between two point charges is proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them. It has the same inverse-square structure as gravitation, with the difference that the electric force can be either attractive or repulsive.
coulomb-law.significance: It is where electromagnetism begins, and it provides the basis for Maxwell's equations and modern electromagnetic theory.

F.description: The force acting between the two charges. Units: newtons (N).

k_e.description: About 8.988×10⁹ N·m²/C². It sets the strength of the electric force.

q_1.description: The charge on the first body. Units: coulombs (C).

q_2.description: The charge on the second body. Like signs repel, unlike signs attract.

r.description: The distance between the two point charges.

r^2.description: It carries the inverse-square law. The farther apart, the more sharply the force falls off.

kinetic-energy.name: Kinetic energy
kinetic-energy.oneLiner: The formula giving the energy of a moving body from its mass and speed
kinetic-energy.description: The kinetic energy formula states that a body of mass m moving at speed v holds an energy of (1/2)mv². Because it goes with the square of the speed, doubling the speed quadruples the energy. It is the heart of the work-energy theorem and a basic building block of the conservation of energy.
kinetic-energy.significance: It is a core component of the conservation of energy and the form of energy used most often in mechanics problems.

K.description: The energy a body has by virtue of its motion. Units: joules (J).

\\frac{1}{2}.description: The factor that appears when the formula is derived by integrating Newton's second law.

m.description: The mass of the moving body. Units: kg.

v.description: The speed at which the body travels. Units: m/s.

v^2.description: Double the speed and the energy quadruples. A non-linear relation.

kinematic-displacement.name: Displacement under constant acceleration
kinematic-displacement.oneLiner: The formula giving the displacement of a body with an initial velocity and constant acceleration as a function of time
kinematic-displacement.description: This is the basic formula for the displacement of a body in straight-line motion under constant acceleration. It adds the distance covered by the initial velocity to the extra distance produced by the acceleration. Together with Newton's second law it is a key tool for solving classical mechanics problems, and it applies to free fall, projectile motion, and much else.
kinematic-displacement.significance: It is the central kinematic formula for describing constant-acceleration motion quantitatively, and the most basic tool for mechanics problems.

s.description: The distance the body has moved. Units: metres (m).

v_0.description: The velocity at the moment the motion starts. Units: m/s.

t.description: How long the motion has been going on. Units: seconds (s).

\\frac{1}{2}.description: The factor that comes out of the integration. It scales the displacement due to the acceleration.

t^2.description: It shows that the displacement due to acceleration goes with the square of the time.

realWorldExamples: Working out how far a freely falling object has dropped after a given number of seconds
Calculating a car's braking distance from the moment the brakes go on until it stops
Calculating the runway length an aeroplane needs for take-off

velocity-acceleration.name: Velocity under constant acceleration
velocity-acceleration.oneLiner: The formula giving how velocity changes with time under constant acceleration
velocity-acceleration.description: This is the most basic kinematic formula, giving the velocity at any moment of straight-line motion under constant acceleration in terms of the initial velocity, the acceleration, and the elapsed time. When the acceleration is constant the velocity changes linearly with time, and the definition of acceleration itself follows from this relation.
velocity-acceleration.significance: It is the most basic kinematic relation quantifying the idea of acceleration, and the starting point for analysing any constant-acceleration motion.

v.description: The velocity at time t. Units: m/s.

v_0.description: The velocity at the moment the motion starts. Units: m/s.

t.description: How long the motion has been going on. Units: seconds (s).

realWorldExamples: Calculating the speed a car reaches 5 seconds after pulling away from the lights
Estimating a skydiver's speed at a given moment after the jump
Working out a rocket's climb rate a set time after launch

velocity-displacement.name: Velocity-displacement relation
velocity-displacement.oneLiner: The formula relating velocity and displacement directly, with no time involved
velocity-displacement.description: This formula eliminates the time variable from straight-line motion under constant acceleration, relating velocity and displacement directly. The square of the final velocity equals the square of the initial velocity plus twice the product of acceleration and displacement. It is especially handy when the time is unknown, and it connects closely to the conservation of energy.
velocity-displacement.significance: Because it links speed and distance without needing the time, it is a key auxiliary tool for mechanics problems.

v^2.description: The square of the final velocity. Units: (m/s)².

v_0^2.description: The square of the initial velocity. Units: (m/s)².

2.description: The factor that appears when the equation of motion is derived.

s.description: The distance the body has moved. Units: metres (m).

realWorldExamples: Working backwards from the braking distance alone to a car's speed just before a crash
Calculating a bullet's muzzle velocity from the barrel length and the acceleration
Working out the speed a roller coaster reaches at a given height

projectile-motion.name: Projectile trajectory equation
projectile-motion.oneLiner: The parabolic equation giving a projectile's path as a function of horizontal distance
projectile-motion.description: This equation gives the trajectory of an object launched with a given initial speed and launch angle. Uniform motion in the horizontal direction combines with constant acceleration under gravity in the vertical direction to form a parabolic path. It is an idealised model that ignores air resistance, but it applies widely, from sports physics to ballistics.
projectile-motion.significance: It established the method of analysing two-dimensional motion by splitting it into horizontal and vertical parts, and it is the basis of ballistics.

y.description: The height above the launch point. Units: metres (m).

x.description: The horizontal distance travelled from the launch point. Units: metres (m).

\\theta.description: The angle between the horizontal and the initial velocity vector.

\\tan\\theta.description: It gives the slope of the trajectory at the start.

g.description: About 9.8 m/s² near the surface of the Earth.

v_0.description: The speed at the moment of launch. Units: m/s.

\\cos^2\\theta.role: Square of the cosine of the launch angle
\\cos^2\\theta.description: It carries the square of the horizontal velocity component.

realWorldExamples: Predicting how far and how high a batted baseball flies
Designing the parabolic arc of a fountain's jet of water
Calculating where a shell fired from a cannon will land

simple-harmonic.name: Simple harmonic motion equation
simple-harmonic.oneLiner: The formula expressing motion that repeats periodically under a restoring force as a sine function
simple-harmonic.description: Simple harmonic motion is the motion of a body subject to a restoring force proportional to its displacement from equilibrium. The displacement is written as a sine (or cosine) function and is described completely by the amplitude, the angular frequency, and the initial phase. It is the basic model for countless oscillations in nature, from a vibrating spring to a swinging pendulum to an LC circuit.
simple-harmonic.significance: It is the most basic model for describing oscillation and wave phenomena, and even complicated periodic motion can be analysed as a superposition of simple harmonic motions.

x.description: How far the body has moved from equilibrium. Units: metres (m).

A.description: The maximum displacement. It measures the size of the oscillation. Units: metres (m).

\\omega.description: How much the phase changes per unit time. Units: rad/s. It relates to the period T as 2π/T.

t.description: How long the motion has been going on. Units: seconds (s).

\\varphi.description: The phase at t=0. It carries the initial conditions.

realWorldExamples: Analysing the period of a clock pendulum swinging back and forth
Modelling the vibration pattern of a guitar string
How a seismometer detects ground vibration

wave-speed.name: Wave speed formula
wave-speed.oneLiner: The relation that a wave's propagation speed equals its frequency times its wavelength
wave-speed.description: The propagation speed of a wave is the distance the wave travels in one second, which equals the number of oscillations per second (the frequency) times the length of one wavelength. It is a basic relation that applies universally to every kind of wave — sound, light, ripples on water.
wave-speed.significance: It is the basic relation applying universally to all wave phenomena, and it underlies acoustics, optics, and communications.

v.description: The speed at which the wave travels through the medium. Units: m/s.

f.description: The number of oscillations per unit time. Units: hertz (Hz).

\\lambda.description: The spatial length of one period. Units: metres (m).

realWorldExamples: Calculating a radio wave's wavelength from its frequency
Determining the wavelength of sound in a medium during an ultrasound scan
Analysing the relation between an instrument's pitch and the length of its resonating tube

ideal-gas-law.name: Ideal gas law
ideal-gas-law.oneLiner: The equation of state relating the pressure, volume, temperature, and amount of an ideal gas
ideal-gas-law.description: The ideal gas law is the equation of state saying that the pressure times the volume of a gas is proportional to the amount of substance times the absolute temperature. It unites Boyle's law, Charles's law, and Avogadro's law in one relation, assuming the ideal conditions of no interaction between molecules and negligible molecular volume.
ideal-gas-law.significance: It is the basic equation of thermodynamics and gas dynamics, and the starting point for understanding the behaviour of real gases approximately.

P.description: How hard the gas pushes on the walls of its container. Units: pascals (Pa).

V.description: The amount of space the gas occupies. Units: cubic metres (m³) or litres (L).

n.description: How much gas there is. Units: moles (mol).

R.description: The ideal gas constant. About 8.314 J/(mol·K).

T.description: The temperature in kelvin. 0 K is absolute zero.

realWorldExamples: Predicting how tyre pressure shifts as the temperature changes
Calculating how a balloon's volume changes when it is heated or cooled
Explaining why a bag of crisps puffs up at high altitude

first-law-thermo.name: First law of thermodynamics
first-law-thermo.oneLiner: The conservation of energy: the change in a system's internal energy equals the heat absorbed minus the work done
first-law-thermo.description: The first law of thermodynamics is the conservation of energy expressed thermodynamically. When a system absorbs heat from its surroundings, its internal energy rises or it does work on the surroundings; energy is neither created nor destroyed. It is the basic constraint on every process involving energy — heat engines, refrigerators, chemical reactions.
first-law-thermo.significance: By establishing that heat and work are different forms of the same energy, it extended the universality of energy conservation into thermodynamics.

\\Delta U.description: How much the system's internal energy changes. The total change in molecular motion and potential energy.

Q.description: The heat the system absorbs from its surroundings. Positive means heat taken in, negative heat given off. Units: joules (J).

W.description: The work the system does on its surroundings. Positive means expansion, negative compression. Units: joules (J).

realWorldExamples: How the heat of burning fuel turns into piston motion in a car engine
How a refrigerator moves heat from inside to outside
Explaining why a gas heats up when compressed adiabatically

schrodinger-eq.name: Schrödinger equation
schrodinger-eq.oneLiner: The fundamental equation of quantum mechanics, describing how a quantum state changes with time
schrodinger-eq.description: The Schrödinger equation is the partial differential equation describing how a wave function changes with time in quantum mechanics. It is the quantum counterpart of Newton's equation of motion in classical mechanics, and it is used to predict the quantum behaviour of atoms, molecules, and solids. The squared magnitude of the wave function gives the probability density of finding the particle.
schrodinger-eq.significance: As the basic equation of motion of quantum mechanics, it underpins atomic structure, chemical bonding, semiconductor physics, and much of modern science.

i.description: The number whose square is -1. It carries the change of phase of the wave function.

\\hbar.description: The Planck constant divided by 2π. About 1.055×10⁻³⁴ J·s.

\\frac{\\partial \\psi}{\\partial t}.role: Time partial derivative of the wave function
\\frac{\\partial \\psi}{\\partial t}.description: It expresses how the wave function changes with time.

\\hat{H}.description: The operator corresponding to the total energy of the system (kinetic plus potential).

\\psi.description: The complex function describing the quantum state. Its squared magnitude is the probability density.

realWorldExamples: Calculating the energy levels of the electron orbitals of a hydrogen atom
Analysing the electronic band structure of a semiconductor
How a scanning tunnelling microscope (STM) works, using quantum tunnelling

de-broglie.name: de Broglie wavelength
de-broglie.oneLiner: The formula showing that every particle has a wave nature, with a wavelength inversely proportional to its momentum
de-broglie.description: According to de Broglie's hypothesis, every particle with mass has wave-like properties, with a wavelength equal to the Planck constant divided by the momentum. This idea of matter waves is the principle behind the electron microscope and was the direct motivation for developing the Schrödinger equation. The de Broglie wavelength of a macroscopic object is far too small to observe, but for microscopic particles such as electrons it has been confirmed experimentally.
de-broglie.significance: By extending wave-particle duality to matter, it supplied the key impetus for the birth of quantum mechanics.

\\lambda.description: The wavelength of the matter wave belonging to the particle. Units: metres (m).

h.description: About 6.626×10⁻³⁴ J·s. The fundamental constant of quantum mechanics.

p.description: The particle's momentum (mass times velocity). Units: kg·m/s.

realWorldExamples: Calculating the wavelength that sets the resolving power of the electron beam in an electron microscope
Analysing crystal structure by neutron diffraction
Precision measurement using the wave nature of atoms in an atom interferometer

boltzmann-dist.name: Boltzmann distribution
boltzmann-dist.oneLiner: The distribution showing that at thermal equilibrium the probability of a particle having a given energy falls off exponentially with that energy
boltzmann-dist.description: The Boltzmann distribution is the basic result of statistical mechanics stating that in a system at thermal equilibrium the probability of a particle having energy E is proportional to e^(-E/kT). The higher the temperature, the more likely the high-energy states are occupied; at low temperature, most particles crowd into the low-energy states. It explains chemical reaction rates, the distribution of electrons in semiconductors, the density profile of the atmosphere, and more.
boltzmann-dist.significance: It is a fundamental principle of statistical mechanics, and it bridges macroscopic thermodynamic laws and the microscopic motion of particles.

P.description: The probability that the particle is in a particular energy state.

e.description: The base of the natural logarithm. About 2.718.

E.description: The energy of the state in question. Units: joules (J).

k.description: About 1.381×10⁻²³ J/K. The constant linking temperature to energy.

T.description: The temperature in kelvin. The higher it is, the more the energy spreads out.

realWorldExamples: Explaining why atmospheric density falls off exponentially with altitude
Predicting how the number of free electrons in a semiconductor changes with temperature
Calculating the fraction of molecules that clear the activation energy barrier in a chemical reaction

lorentz-transform.name: Lorentz transformation of time
lorentz-transform.oneLiner: The formula of special relativity for transforming the time coordinate between inertial frames
lorentz-transform.description: The Lorentz transformation converts spacetime coordinates between two inertial frames moving at constant velocity relative to each other. The time equation shows that the time in one frame depends on the space coordinate in the other, which is the mathematical statement of the relativity of simultaneity. It is the root of relativistic effects such as time dilation and length contraction.
lorentz-transform.significance: By replacing the Galilean transformation, it established the mathematical foundation of special relativity.

t'.description: The time coordinate in the moving observer's frame.

\\gamma.description: 1/sqrt(1 - v²/c²). It grows as the speed approaches that of light.

t.description: The time coordinate in the rest frame.

v.description: The relative velocity between the two frames. Units: m/s.

x.description: The position in the rest frame. It shows that space enters the transformation of time.

c^2.role: Square of the speed of light
c^2.description: The constant of proportionality of the spacetime transformation. It sets how time and space mix.

realWorldExamples: The clock corrections applied to GPS satellites (accounting for relativistic time dilation)
Observing the extended lifetime of fast particles in an accelerator
Explaining how muons manage to reach the ground from the upper atmosphere

gauss-law.name: Gauss's law
gauss-law.oneLiner: The first of Maxwell's equations: the divergence of the electric field produced by a charge distribution is proportional to the charge density
gauss-law.description: Gauss's law, the first of the four Maxwell equations, states that the divergence of the electric field — how much it spreads out at a point — equals the charge density there divided by the permittivity of free space. It is the mathematical statement that charge is the source of the electric field, with the field flowing out of positive charge and into negative charge. It is especially useful for finding the field of a highly symmetric charge distribution concisely.
gauss-law.discoverer: Carl Friedrich Gauss / James Clerk Maxwell
gauss-law.significance: As one of the four fundamental equations of electromagnetism (Maxwell's equations), it fixes the relation between charge and the electric field.

\\nabla \\cdot \\mathbf{E}.description: The differential operation saying how much the electric field spreads out from, or converges on, a point.

\\rho.description: The charge per unit volume. Units: C/m³.

\\varepsilon_0.description: About 8.854×10⁻¹² F/m. The constant setting the strength of the electric field in a vacuum.

realWorldExamples: Calculating the electric field at the surface of a conducting sphere
Deriving the uniform field inside a parallel-plate capacitor
Explaining why the electric field inside a charged conductor is zero
